prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or restart ciprofloxacin or any other fluoroquinolone.
Do not use an aminoglycoside, a macrolide or IV magnesium for the infection or for electrolyte replacement.
Do not prescribe a penicillin (documented rash), including amoxicillin or pivmecillinam.
Do not attribute the worsening to the urinary infection alone without recognizing the fluoroquinolone trigger.
Use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring if she is intubated.
required_recommendations: Treat the E. coli cystitis with an MG-safe, non-penicillin antibiotic guided by susceptibility, for example nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily for 5 days (creatinine normal) or single-dose fosfomycin 3 g.

Admit to an ICU or high-dependency unit: MEP below 40 cmH2O and MIP close to -30 cmH2O with bulbar weakness meet impending-crisis criteria; repeat FVC, MIP and MEP every 4-6 hours and plan intubation if FVC falls below 15-20 mL/kg, MIP is weaker than -30 cmH2O, PaCO2 rises or she cannot clear secretions.
Start IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days or plasma exchange (5 exchanges) for the impending crisis.

Do not escalate pyridostigmine further (return to 60 mg four times daily, hold if intubated because of secretions); continue azathioprine and prednisone, increasing prednisone only under respiratory monitoring.
Keep nil by mouth for thin liquids until a formal swallow assessment, with aspiration precautions.
Replace metoprolol with an antihypertensive without neuromuscular effect (for example amlodipine) once stable.

MG had been stable for months; the step change began acutely after ciprofloxacin rather than over weeks.

Metoprolol has been on the regimen for years without prior MG worsening; contributes potential additive NMJ risk but the temporal trigger is fluoroquinolone initiation 4 days ago, not the beta-blocker.
Known AChR-positive MG for 6 years; normal baseline CMAPs without post-exercise facilitation, preserved reflexes and no autonomic symptoms.

She increased pyridostigmine to five doses a day (300 mg), but there are no muscarinic signs (pupils 3 mm, heart rate 84, no sweating, hypersalivation or diarrhea) and the weakness preceded the increase.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute worsening of known AChR-positive MG beginning 24-36 hours after ciprofloxacin was started, in a patient stable for months: a fluoroquinolone-precipitated exacerbation.
Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for worsening of myasthenia gravis; stopping the drug is the first step.
MEP 38 cmH2O and MIP -32 cmH2O (from -52) with dysphagia, nasal regurgitation and a weak cough: impending myasthenic crisis needing ICU-level monitoring and IVIG or plasma exchange.
Leukocytosis, raised CRP and pyuria reflect a real cystitis, but there is no fever and procalcitonin is normal; the infection needs an MG-safe antibiotic chosen by susceptibility.
The urine grows ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli; with a penicillin allergy, nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin are the safe choices.
Pyridostigmine at about 240-300 mg/day without muscarinic signs makes a cholinergic crisis unlikely; further escalation would add secretions without benefit.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 60-year-old woman with a 6-year history of AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of rapidly progressive worsening of her baseline MG symptoms. Her MG had been well-controlled on pyridostigmine 60 mg four times daily, prednisone 10 mg daily, and azathioprine 100 mg daily, with her last clinic visit 3 months ago documenting MGFA Class IIa with mild, stable bulbar symptoms and bedside respiratory measurements within her usual range.

Four days before admission, she was evaluated by her primary care physician for dysuria and urinary frequency. Urinalysis was abnormal and a clinical diagnosis of uncomplicated urinary tract infection was made. Because of a documented penicillin allergy, she was prescribed ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily. Within 24-36 hours of starting the antibiotic, she noticed her right eyelid drooping more than usual. By day 2, she had significant bilateral ptosis, nasal dysarthria after brief speaking, and difficulty swallowing thin liquids. By day 3, she was unable to lift her arms above her head and required assistance to rise from a chair. Her husband noticed she seemed more breathless walking to the bathroom. She has taken all her pyridostigmine doses as prescribed and increased the frequency herself (now attempting five times daily) without improvement.

She denies fever, chills, rigors, or flank pain. She completed the UTI evaluation but has had ongoing mild dysuria. She has no new rash, joint pain, chest pain, or palpitations. She has not taken any new medications other than the ciprofloxacin. She denies aminoglycoside use and has not received any infusions or injections. She explicitly recalls that a neurologist warned her to avoid certain antibiotics but she did not remember which ones and the prescription was filled without that history being checked. There has been no recent illness, travel, or vaccination.
